posts.title: Loneliness and the cigarette comparison
posts.insight: The comparison between loneliness and smoking appears in a 2010 review that mostly measured other social ties, not loneliness. Studies of loneliness itself find a smaller link with earlier death than for social isolation, and one English cohort found no independent link after allowing for health.
posts.angle: Test a familiar slogan against its source and later evidence; argue that loneliness deserves attention for the distress it causes, without a cigarette comparison that overstates certainty.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the description of the 2010 review and later studies is empirical finding; 'we should drop the comparison and take loneliness seriously for its distress' is ethical judgement and clinical interpretation.

captions.x:
You have probably heard that loneliness is as bad for you as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. A smoking comparison does appear in a 2010 review of 148 studies. Most of those studies measured something other than loneliness.

They measured marriage, the size of social networks, support and involvement with others. Loneliness itself supplied only 8 of several hundred results. The smoking bar in the chart was fewer than 15 a day, taken from a different review of different people.

The largest recent reviews of loneliness on its own still find it linked with earlier death, but less strongly than social isolation (having little contact with others). These are observational studies. In one English study of about 6,500 people aged 52 and over, loneliness was no longer linked with death once health at the start was allowed for.

We should drop the cigarette line. Loneliness is painful to live with, and that is reason enough to take it seriously.
captions.linkedin:
You have probably heard that loneliness is as bad for you as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. It is worth checking where a comparison like that comes from before repeating it.

A smoking comparison appears in a 2010 review that pooled 148 studies of about 309,000 people, followed for 7.5 years on average. People with stronger social relationships were more likely to be alive at the end of follow-up. A chart set the size of that link beside other risk factors, including smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes a day. The chart compared numbers from different reviews of different people; it was not a head-to-head test.

Most of the pooled results measured marriage, social networks, support and involvement with others. Loneliness itself was measured in only 8 of several hundred results. Within those 8, less loneliness was still linked with better survival.

What happens when loneliness is studied on its own?

1. A 2015 review of studies that allowed for other factors found loneliness linked with higher odds of dying during follow-up (odds ratio 1.26), about the same as for social isolation and living alone.
2. In the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (about 6,500 people aged 52 and over, followed for about 7 years), lonely people were more likely to die at first. After allowing for age, background and health at the start, loneliness was no longer linked with death (hazard ratio 0.92, interval 0.78 to 1.09); social isolation still was.
3. Reviews from 2023 and 2025, one in older adults, find loneliness linked with earlier death, less strongly than isolation, with wide variation between studies.

All of this is observational. None of it shows that loneliness causes death, or that it does not.

My reading: we should drop the cigarette comparison. It borrows certainty that the studies do not give. The ELSA authors wrote that reducing loneliness is important for quality of life and well-being. Loneliness is painful to live with, and that is reason enough to ask about it and help.
captions.bluesky:
A smoking comparison appears in a 2010 review of social ties. Only 8 of its several hundred results measured loneliness, and the bar was fewer than 15 cigarettes a day.

Recent large reviews link loneliness with earlier death, less than isolation.

Loneliness is painful: reason enough to help.

posts.title: Did not attend is a finding
posts.insight: In Scottish GP data, people over 90 and people in the most deprived areas were among the most likely to miss appointments repeatedly, and missed appointments were linked with higher mortality. A missed appointment is a warning sign worth a phone call.
posts.angle: The record counts the absence and not the reason; for an older person a missed appointment should prompt contact before discharge back to the GP.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the risk patterns are empirical findings (observational); the call to phone before discharging is clinical interpretation and judgement.

captions.x:
A "did not attend" code records that someone was absent. It records nothing about why.

In Scottish GP records from 2013 to 2016 (550,083 patients), people over 90 and people in the most deprived areas were among the most likely to miss appointments repeatedly, even after allowing for how many appointments they made. Young adults aged 16 to 30 were also at higher risk, and how practices ran their appointments counted too.

A linked study found people with more long-term conditions missed more appointments, and people who missed appointments were more likely to die in the following months. That is a warning sign, not proof of cause.

My view: for an older person, a missed appointment should prompt a phone call to ask what got in the way, before any letter discharging them back to the GP.
captions.linkedin:
A "did not attend" code records that someone was absent. It records nothing about why.

Two Scottish studies of GP records suggest the absence itself tells us something.

In the first, covering 550,083 patients from 2013 to 2016, people over 90 and people living in the most deprived areas were among the most likely to miss appointments repeatedly. This held after allowing for how many appointments each person made. Young adults aged 16 to 30 were also at higher risk, and practice factors, such as how appointments were organised, also made a substantial difference.

In the second, people with more long-term conditions missed more appointments, and people who missed appointments were more likely to die in the following months. The link was strongest in people with long-term mental health conditions. The authors call missed appointments a risk marker. The studies do not show that missing an appointment causes death, and they cover all ages, not only older people.

What should a clinic do with that?

My view is that for an older person, a missed appointment should prompt contact before any discharge letter. The questions are practical ones:

1. Did the letter or text reach them, and could they read or hear it?
2. Could they get there?
3. Do they depend on someone else to bring them?
4. Has something changed at home or in their health?

These questions come from judgement, not from these studies, which did not record reasons. A discharge letter after missed appointments treats the absence as a choice. For some of the people most at risk, it may not have been one.
captions.bluesky:
In Scottish GP records, people over 90, young adults and people in the most deprived areas were among the most likely to miss appointments repeatedly. At all ages, missing appointments was linked with more deaths: a warning sign, not a cause.

Phone and ask why before any discharge letter.

posts.title: Phone calls that listen
posts.insight: In a 4-week trial, regular phone calls from briefly trained young callers who listened and let people choose the topics reduced loneliness scores and symptoms of anxiety and depression in homebound adults. Whether the benefit lasts is unknown.
posts.angle: What the programme did, in detail, and an honest reading of its modest, short-term result.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial results are empirical findings; the view that services could try this now, with follow-up measured, is clinical interpretation.

captions.x:
Sixteen young people aged 17 to 23, mostly students, with about 2 hours of training, phoned people who were getting Meals on Wheels at home in Texas. They were taught to listen and to let the person choose what to talk about. No scripts.

The 2020 trial randomly assigned 240 people, aged 27 to 101, to calls or no calls. More than half lived alone. Each person was assigned to one caller. Calls came 5 days in the first week, then 2 to 5 a week as the person chose.

After 4 weeks, loneliness scores (3 to 9 scale) fell from 6.5 to 5.2 with calls and from 6.5 to 6.3 without. Anxiety and depression symptoms improved. A second loneliness questionnaire showed no clear difference.

The trial lasted only 4 weeks. Nobody knows if the benefit lasts. It is cheap enough to try and measure.
captions.linkedin:
Sixteen young people aged 17 to 23, mostly students, with about 2 hours of training, phoned people who were getting Meals on Wheels at home in Texas. They were taught to listen, to let the person choose what to talk about, and to ask about what the person raised. They had no scripts and no therapy training.

The trial, run in the summer of 2020, randomly assigned 240 homebound people to regular calls or no calls. They were aged 27 to 101; about 6 in 10 were 65 or over, more than half lived alone, and all had at least one long-term condition. People with cognitive impairment were not included.

How it worked:

1. Each person was assigned to one caller, who looked after 6 to 9 people.
2. Calls came 5 days in the first week, at a time the person chose.
3. After that, people chose between 2 and 5 calls a week. Most (58 in 100) kept 5.

After 4 weeks, loneliness scores on a 3 to 9 scale fell from 6.5 to 5.2 in people who got calls, and from 6.5 to 6.3 in those who did not. Symptoms of anxiety and depression also improved. Among people with at least mild anxiety at the start, the share still anxious fell from 50 in 100 to 36 in 100 with calls, and stayed about 50 in 100 without.

The limits are real. A second loneliness questionnaire did not show a clear difference. Physical health did not change. More people dropped out of the call group (13) than the comparison group (1). The trial lasted 4 weeks, during the pandemic, and does not show whether the listening style or simply being called made the difference. Reviews have not yet found enough evidence to judge telephone programmes as a group.

My reading: this is a cheap, specific programme that services could try now, as long as they measure what happens after the first month.

More posts in the Care that works series look at one programme at a time: what it did and what it showed.

posts.title: The partner left at home
posts.insight: In a US study, carers of people with dementia were as depressed and anxious after their relative moved into a care home as before, and spouses were hit hardest. The partner who stays at home needs their own conversation.
posts.angle: The care home plan is built around the resident; the husband or wife at home, who often still visits daily and helps with care, is handed over to nobody.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the Schulz 2004 findings are empirical; offering the partner their own conversation is ethical judgement, not a tested intervention (Brooks 2018).

captions.x:
When your husband or wife moves into a care home, the plan is written for them. Who asks how you are?

In a US study of family carers of people with dementia, carers were just as depressed and anxious after their relative moved into a care home as before. Nearly half were at risk of clinical depression afterwards. Spouses were hit hardest: almost half visited every day and still helped with their partner's physical care.

The study is from 1996 to 2000, in the US, and about dementia. Only a few small trials have tested support after a move, without clear effects.

I think the partner at home should be offered their own conversation. If that is you, ask: who will check how I am managing? And how does the fees assessment treat our home and my income if I stay in the house?
captions.linkedin:
When your husband or wife moves into a care home, the plan is written for them. Who asks how you are?

A US study followed 1,222 family carers of people with dementia between 1996 and 2000. During 18 months, 180 of their relatives moved into long-term care. The carers were just as depressed and anxious after the move as they had been while caring at home. Nearly half were at risk of clinical depression afterwards.

Husbands and wives were hit hardest. Almost half of spouses visited every day and still helped with their partner's physical care during those visits.

So the move ends one kind of caring and starts another. The person at home may also be living alone for the first time in decades, with unfamiliar questions about money.

Can support help? Only a few small trials have tested support for carers after a care home move, and they did not show clear effects on depression or burden. So what follows is judgement, not a tested treatment.

I think the partner who stays at home should be offered their own conversation, separate from the plan for the resident. If that is you, these are fair questions to ask before or soon after the move:

1. Who will check how I am managing, and when?
2. How does the fees assessment treat our home and my income if I stay in the house?
3. Can I keep helping with care in the ways I want to, and stop where I need to?

The study is American, over 20 years old, and about dementia carers. The questions still apply wherever you are.
captions.bluesky:
In a US study, carers of people with dementia were as depressed and anxious after their relative moved into a care home as before. Spouses were hit hardest; almost half still visited daily and helped with care.

posts.title: In a heatwave, check on the person who lives alone
posts.insight: In past heatwaves, the older people most likely to die were confined to bed, did not leave home each day, lived alone or slept on a top floor. Social contact and ways to cool down were linked with survival.
posts.angle: The heat risk profile is also an isolation and housing profile; a daily check and a cooler room are practical protection.
posts.position_basis: mixed: risk factors are empirical findings from case-control studies; daily checks are a judgement drawn from them, not tested in trials.

captions.x:
In the 1995 Chicago heatwave, the people most likely to die were those confined to bed or who did not leave home each day. Living on a top floor and living alone also raised the risk.

Having friends nearby or group activities, working air conditioning and access to transport were linked with lower risk.

In the 2003 French heatwave, among people aged 65 and over at home, being unable to get about, a poorly insulated home and sleeping on the top floor under the roof were linked with dying. Dressing lightly and ways to cool down were linked with surviving.

This advice comes from studies of who died, not from trials of checking. Still: in hot weather, if you know an older person who is alone and rarely goes out, call or visit every day.
captions.linkedin:
In the 1995 Chicago heatwave, the people most likely to die were those confined to bed or who did not leave home each day. Living on the top floor of a building and living alone also raised the risk.

The study compared 339 people who died with 339 neighbours of similar age who survived. Having social contacts, such as friends in the area or group activities, was linked with lower risk. So were working air conditioning and access to transport.

Eight years later, a study of the August 2003 heatwave in France looked at people aged 65 and over living at home. Being unable to get about, living in a poorly insulated home, and sleeping on the top floor right under the roof were linked with dying. Dressing lightly and using ways to cool down were linked with surviving.

Put together, the people at highest risk in a heatwave are often the same people who are most isolated: at home all day, alone, high up in the building, unable to get out.

These are studies of who died, not trials of what prevents death. My judgement is that they still point to simple steps. In hot weather, for an older person who is alone or rarely goes out:

1. Call or visit every day.
2. Help them move to a cooler, lower room to sleep if they can.
3. Encourage light clothing and whatever cooling they have: shade, fans, cool water.
4. Arrange a lift or company if they need to get out.

If that person is you, it is reasonable to ask someone to check on you each day until the heat passes.
captions.bluesky:
In the Chicago (1995) and French (2003) heatwaves, people who were confined to bed, rarely left home, lived alone or slept on a top floor were more likely to die. Contact with others and ways to cool down were linked with survival.

In hot weather, check daily on anyone alone.
captions.threads:
In the 1995 Chicago heatwave, people confined to bed or who did not leave home each day were most likely to die. Living alone and on a top floor also raised the risk. Friends nearby, air conditioning and transport were linked with lower risk.

France in 2003 showed a similar pattern for older people at home.

These studies looked at who died, not at trials of checking. Still, in hot weather, call or visit an older person who is alone every day.

posts.title: Welfare advice in the GP surgery
posts.insight: Welfare rights advice offered in health settings consistently leaves people better off financially. The health effects are plausible but poorly measured, which is an evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit.
posts.angle: A model of care with an honest reading of what is established and what is not.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the financial and health findings are empirical (low-quality studies); offering a route to advice and measuring health effects better is clinical interpretation and judgement.

captions.x:
Money advice in a GP surgery has one result every study in a 2022 review agreed on: people ended up better off.

The review found 14 UK studies of welfare rights advice offered in GP surgeries and other health settings. All reported improved financial security. Some reported better mental health, and some people said their physical health improved.

Most studies were small case studies of poor quality, and they covered all ages. So the health effects are poorly measured: a gap in the evidence, rather than evidence of no benefit.

My view: services that see older people on low incomes should offer a route to welfare rights advice, and better studies should measure what it does for health.
captions.linkedin:
Money advice in a GP surgery has one result every study in a 2022 review agreed on: people ended up better off.

The review, by Reece and colleagues, found 14 UK studies from 2010 to 2020 of welfare rights advice placed in GP surgeries and other health settings. All reported improved financial security for the people who used it. Some reported better mental health. Several reported that people felt their physical health had improved.

The weaknesses are clear. The studies included one non-randomised controlled trial, one pilot randomised trial, one before-and-after study, three qualitative studies and eight case studies. The authors warned that, given the generally poor quality of the studies, care must be taken in drawing firm conclusions. They also covered all ages, not only older people.

A second 2022 review of UK advice services reached a similar reading: better mental health and wellbeing are commonly attributed to advice, earlier reviews described the evidence on health as weak, and placing advice in health settings looks promising.

So two things are true at once. The financial gain was reported consistently, though by mostly weak studies. The health gain is plausible and under-measured. Weak evidence is a reason to measure better, not a reason to conclude there is no benefit.

My view: health services that see older people on low incomes should offer a clear route to welfare rights advice. We already ask about pain, falls and medicines. Asking whether someone can afford to heat the house and eat well, and knowing where to send them, belongs in the same conversation. The next studies should measure health outcomes properly.
captions.bluesky:
A 2022 review of 14 UK studies found welfare rights advice in GP surgeries and other health settings left people better off financially every time.

Health effects were poorly measured: a gap, not proof of no benefit.

Offer older people on low incomes a route to advice.

posts.title: Ask about sex, especially at a medicines review
posts.insight: Many people in their 70s and 80s are sexually active, sexual problems are common, and few have discussed sex with a doctor. Some common medicines cause sexual side effects that people rarely report unless asked.
posts.angle: Not asking is a default that hides treatable problems and medicine side effects; ask, particularly when starting or reviewing antidepressants.
posts.position_basis: mixed: prevalence and side-effect data are empirical; the instruction to ask is clinical interpretation.

captions.x:
About 1 in 4 people aged 75 to 85 in a US national survey had been sexually active with a partner in the past year: about 4 in 10 men and 1 in 6 women. About half of sexually active people had at least one sexual problem that bothered them.

Only about 4 in 10 men and 1 in 5 women had talked about sex with a doctor since turning 50.

Many common antidepressants, such as sertraline, citalopram and venlafaxine, cause sexual side effects, and people tend not to mention them unless asked directly.

Ask. A medicines review is a natural moment. But do not assume the blood pressure tablet is to blame: in one trial of five blood pressure medicines, only chlorthalidone clearly differed from placebo, and only over the first 2 years.
captions.linkedin:
About 1 in 4 people aged 75 to 85 in a US national survey had been sexually active with a partner in the past year: about 4 in 10 men and 1 in 6 women.

The survey interviewed 3,005 people aged 57 to 85 in 2005 to 2006. About half of those who were sexually active had at least one sexual problem that bothered them. Only about 4 in 10 men and 1 in 5 women said they had talked about sex with a doctor since turning 50. The authors noted that both patients and doctors were reluctant to raise it.

English data point the same way. In the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (2012 to 2013), a sizeable minority of men and women were still sexually active in their 70s and 80s. Among those who were, about 4 in 10 men reported erection problems and about 1 in 3 women reported difficulty with arousal.

Why this belongs in the medicines review:

1. Sexual side effects are common with many widely used antidepressants, such as sertraline, citalopram and venlafaxine. People tend not to mention them unless asked directly. Some, such as mirtazapine, did not show a clear difference from placebo.
2. In a blinded trial of five blood pressure medicines, men on chlorthalidone had more new erection problems over 2 years than men on placebo: about 17 in 100 compared with 8 in 100. The other four did not clearly differ from placebo, so a new problem should not automatically be blamed on the blood pressure tablet.

These studies have limits: the US survey is about 20 years old, and the medicine studies were not in older people specifically.

The teaching point: ask about sexual health in older patients, in plain words, and ask again when you start or review a medicine that can affect it.
